text:
Tonight on LWC: Hayden Breaks With KCSO, Norris Gets Checked & Counties First

There’s a lot happening in North Idaho this week, and tonight we’re digging into the records, the rulings and a few stories you probably won’t hear anywhere else.

Hayden files for “divorce” from KCSO. The Hayden City Council voted Tuesday not to renew its law-enforcement contract with the Kootenai County Sheriff’s Office for 2027. The council’s discussion included questions about cost, accountability and data—including a consultant’s finding that 61.2% of deputy working hours were unaccounted for. Councilmembers emphasized that their concerns weren’t directed at the individual deputies serving Hayden. (CDAPress) What does ending the policing contract actually mean for Hayden—and what happens next?

Then, did Sheriff Bob Norris put the cart before the horse? We’re revisiting the undersheriff salary issue and the BOCC meeting where Commissioner Bruce Mattare pressed Norris over seeking a higher salary for a prospective undersheriff before the commissioners had approved the increase. We’ll also get into Mattare’s email and what it tells us about the county’s position.

The verdict is in on Summer Bushnell’s appeal. The Idaho Supreme Court unanimously upheld the civil judgment against Bushnell in the Eric Posey defamation case. The court said most of the issues she raised lacked adequate argument or authority and described inaccuracies in her briefing as “pervasive and egregious.” The court even raised questions about whether generative AI may have been used, something Bushnell denied. We’ll break down what the ruling actually says and where the case stands now.

And then there’s Samuel Michael Johnson and the $1,000 challenge. After Johnson began making serious public accusations about Dan, Dan challenged him to substantiate them and offered $1,000 if he could. Johnson said he’d take the money “in $20s.” Then the deadline came and went. We’ll show you what was alleged, what the challenge required, and what happened afterward.

We’re changing gears for “5 Things You May Not Know About Dawna.” After a local public figure recently spotted Dawna in a commercial and decided her professional work was somehow worthy of a political complaint, Dan has questions. We’ll have some fun with it while pulling back the curtain on what Dawna actually does professionally—and why seeing her pop up in an ad has absolutely nothing to do with North Idaho politics.

Special Guest: Matt Hawkins — Counties First

Tonight we’re also joined by Matt Hawkins, author of Counties First: A House Divided: Restoring the Representative Government Guaranteed to Every State. Hawkins advocates restoring county-based representation in state senates and argues that doing so would strengthen local representation and popular sovereignty; his public writing emphasizes that he views the proposal as a question of representation rather than party politics. (LinkedIn)

We’ll talk with Matt about the history behind his argument, what he believes changed in American representative government, why he puts counties at the center of the solution, and what his proposal would mean in practice.

🎙️ Liberty Without Compromise with Dan & Dawna Wilson
🔴 LIVE Wednesday — 7 PM PT | 10 PM ET

text:
Israel apologized immediately and through official diplomatic channels after the June 8, 1967 attack on the USS Liberty, describing it as a tragic wartime error of mistaken identity. 

Israeli officials notified the United States the same day that Israeli aircraft and torpedo boats had attacked the ship by mistake, believing it to be an Egyptian vessel. They offered “abject apologies” and assistance. 

Prime Minister Levi Eshkol sent a message to President Lyndon Johnson expressing “profound condolences” and asking that sympathy be conveyed to the families. Foreign Minister Abba Eban stated he was “deeply mortified and grieved by the tragic accident.” Chargé d’affaires Ephraim Evron also sent personal condolences. 

On June 8 and again on June 10, Israeli Ambassador Avraham Harman delivered formal diplomatic notes to Secretary of State Dean Rusk. The June 10 note said the Government of Israel “deeply regrets this tragic accident,” renewed its “sincere expression of deep regret,” offered condolences to the United States and the bereaved families, and stated that Israel was “prepared to make amends for the tragic loss of life and material damage.” Subsequent notes reiterated that Israel had immediately assumed responsibility for the “tragic error” and conveyed “apologies and deep regret.” 

 It later paid compensation totaling roughly $13 million (in then-year dollars): about $3.32 million in 1968 for the families of those killed, $3.57 million in 1969 for the wounded, and $6 million in the early 1980s for damage to the ship. The two governments formally closed the compensation claims in the 1980s. 

The U.S. government publicly accepted the apology and the explanation of error at the official level.

News Flashback

Jan-March 2026

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Jev is fast and cheap, but why?

Our CTO spent two days testing it on a $3,500 desktop at home, not on Trioma’s GPUs. He started with 34 handwritten requests, then ran 1,934 real production requests.

What we found changes how you should look at Jev.
The numbers are below👇

Everyone is talking about Jev, the new "System One" model from TypeSafe AI. The claims are loud: up to 400× faster than GPT, up to 10,000× cheaper, a decision in 70-500 milliseconds, errors that are "mathematically impossible", input at four cents per million tokens, output free. Some people say it labelled ten thousand emails in twenty minutes for a dollar. Others say that on real pipelines the effect is "not zero, but very weak".

When something sounds like that, someone should check. So our CTO and co-founder, Dmitriy, did: on a desktop box in his home office, over two days. This is his review, published as he wrote it, including the parts where he loses.

TL;DR
- The speed and the "impossible errors" come from the form of the question (one token, a decoder grammar), not from the model. Any model you already run can do it.
- With zero labels, Jev and a plain 27B open-weight model tie on accuracy: 0.770 vs 0.769.
- Chain-of-thought reasoning doesn't help on these tasks. It costs 75× more for the same answers.
- What Jev really sells is calibrated confidence with no labels: it routes 4× more traffic automatically than raw model probabilities do.
- 50-100 labelled rows from your own logs close that gap.
- On batched questions Jev is 2.6× faster than the box. On cost, the desktop box loses to Jev; a $2,000 gaming card would win (projected).
- Classification is the one task where local hardware catches up completely, and it's also the task that ships the most data out. Privacy is the real argument, not speed.

The rig
Deliberately nothing special: an ASUS Ascent GX10, a $3,500 desktop box the size of a thick book, 128 GB of unified memory, running an off-the-shelf 27B open-weight model in BF16 on vLLM. It writes prose at 4.5 tokens per second: slow enough to make coffee while it finishes a paragraph. If the trick works here, it works anywhere.

Credit first
Jev calls itself a System One model, after Kahneman: fast, intuitive answers. The insight is right. Most of what we ask language models to do isn't writing. It's choosing: which pipeline, which tool, approve or escalate, toxic or fine. Those questions don't need an essay. They need an answer.
TypeSafe offers three primitives for this: Choice (pick one of a set), Score (rate on a scale) and Noul (how true is this, from 0 to 1), asked in batches against one shared state, with probabilities attached.

The trick behind the speed
When a model picks one option out of five, the useful output is one token. A letter. Everything else in {"choice":"D"} is packaging, and decode time scales with output tokens. Ask for one token and read the probabilities straight from the logits: you get a decision plus probabilities from any model, with no training.
"Type errors are mathematically impossible" isn't magic either. It's the decoder. If the output grammar only allows A-E, a sixth answer can't exist. In vLLM that's one line, guided_choice. And TypeSafe's documented limit of 255 options looks a lot like one byte per class.

About the famous 70 milliseconds
That's server time. The road to the server isn't in the ad. Measured from Singapore, a TLS handshake to https://t.co/bnK75l7pXC took 367 milliseconds: one AWS region in Oregon, no edge termination. The same handshake to a Cloudflare-fronted API took 19. Where a model lives matters as much as how fast it thinks. (Part two measures the real end-to-end figure: about 460 ms. Anycast saves the handshake; it doesn't save the ocean.)

Test one: 34 requests
Five routes (text, new image, edit image, video, audio), eight requests deliberately ambiguous. Each asked two ways.

One token: 493 ms, 85.3% accuracy
JSON object: 1,381 ms, 85.3%
Pretty JSON with schema: 3,735 ms, 85.3%

Identical answers on all 34, mistakes included. Six of seven tokens were paid for nothing.

Why a desktop box can play this game: physics
27 billion parameters × 2 bytes = 54 GB of weights. The chip reads memory at 273 GB/s. 273 ÷ 54 ≈ 5 tokens per second; measured, 4.5. Decoding is a memory-read problem, not a math problem.
So eight decisions in parallel read the weights once: 308 ms per decision alone, 110-155 ms in a batch of eight (throughput, not latency; it drifted between runs, and he says so). And putting the context first and the question last means a second question to the same context drops from 3,025 to 341 ms. The cache does the rest.

"But surely it needs to think?"
Chain-of-thought on, 16 cases. With reasoning: 12 of 16 correct, 36.3 seconds, about 172 tokens each. One token: 12 of 16 correct, half a second. Reasoning didn't remove the errors. It rearranged them, at 75× the price. On a System One task the answer is already in the first pass.

Where he lost
Raw LLM probabilities are overconfident. In the "95-99.9% sure" bucket the model was right 40% of the time. If you route on a threshold, that's unusable. This is exactly what TypeSafe fixes with training, and a prompt can't.

Round two: 2,000 real requests, and Jev itself
Then he caught himself cheating: 34 prompts he wrote himself, none in English, median 42 characters, against real traffic that is twice as long, mostly English and messier. So round two: about 2,000 anonymised real requests, and a real head-to-head with Jev via OpenRouter. The run cost 3.5 cents and took seven minutes.
First, what does "nothing fancy" score?
- Always guess the most common class: 0.207
- Keyword rules: 0.490
- Naive Bayes on word counts, a 1960s algorithm, with - labels: 0.761
- Zero-shot 27B model, no labels: 0.703

A zero-shot LLM is worth about 650 labelled examples. That's a number you can put in a budget.
Head-to-head, same prompts, same context, same rules, zero labels: Jev 0.770, his model with five yes/no probes 0.769. A statistical tie (p = 0.89). Detailed class descriptions helped Jev by 6.5 points and hurt his model by 4; there is no universal prompt.
With about 1,500 labels, his stack (probes plus a measured confusion matrix) reaches 0.792 against Jev's 0.770 (p = 0.0016). And a fun one: Naive Bayes and the 27B model, on equal data, are a dead heat (p = 0.67). Combined, they reach 0.834. They are wrong in different places.

Where Jev is really better
Confidence you can trust with zero labels. Share of traffic you can route automatically at 5% error or less:

Raw probes: 10.5%
Jev: 42.8%
Probes plus confusion matrix (needs labels): 59.0%

That's the real product: not accuracy, which is ordinary, but calibrated uncertainty out of the box. It's honest value, and he says so.

How many labels to close the gap yourself? About 50 gets you level on average; 100-200 puts you comfortably above with far less variance. And those aren't hand labels: they're rows from your own logs saying which pipeline actually ran.

Their real form: batches
Eight questions in one call take the time of one, cost a quarter of eight separate calls, and gave the same answers in 39 of 40 cases. The Score primitive returns a full distribution plus a confidence; on an unclear case it said 0.07. It knows when it doesn't know.
End-to-end from Singapore, real calls: one question, box 364 ms vs Jev 441; eight questions, box 942 vs Jev 361. Their time is flat: all answers come out of one pass. His grows: each question is a separate call. On their form they win by 2.6×.

Hardware, not intelligence
Decode floor equals weight bytes divided by memory bandwidth, and that transfers across GPUs. Measured on the GX10: 118 ms per question. Projected from bandwidth: about 8 ms on an RTX 4090 at INT4, about 6.7 ms on an H200. Strip the network out of Jev's 361 ms and you get roughly 7.6 ms per question: datacenter class. No miracle. They stand on better hardware. The box lost on hardware, not on method.

Economics, counted to the end
- Jev: $0.000022 per decision one at a time, $0.0000041 in batches of eight
- The GX10, amortised over three years plus power: $0.000006

So the desktop box is more expensive than Jev batched. He didn't hide it. A $2,000 gaming card, projected from bandwidth (INT4 accuracy unmeasured), comes to about 17× cheaper than Jev. Datacenter cards beat Jev by only 1.2-1.5×: their price roughly tracks their hardware.

The most expensive lesson in the write-up: don't buy a box with "AI" written on it. Buy memory bandwidth. 128 GB at 273 GB/s is the wrong shape for this job; a gaming card has four times the bandwidth for half the price. GB/s per dollar is the one number that sets the price of a decision.

What nobody prices in
Someone labelled ten thousand Gmail messages with Jev in twenty minutes for about a dollar. That's also ten thousand emails on someone else's server. Classification needs the full text (you can't ask "is this spam?" without showing the email), and it's bulk by nature (one labelling of an archive is the whole archive). The cheapest task quietly becomes the biggest data export you'll ever do.

And classification is the one LLM task where a local box catches up completely. For writing you may need a frontier model you can't host; that trade-off is real. For a one-token decision there is none. The task where you most want data to stay home is the one where staying home is free.

The recipe, if you build it yourself
- One call, one token: max_tokens=1, logprobs on. Read the probabilities from the logits.
- Five yes/no probes ("is this pipeline X?") instead of one five-way choice.
- Forbid impossible classes: no attachment means it can't be "edit". Two lines, plus five points, no labels needed.
- No labels? Stop here, at 0.769.
- A hundred labels or more? Add the confusion-matrix decoder. That's what turns raw probabilities into a threshold you can rely on.
- Don't route everything. Escalate the unsure half.

Almost none of this is new: one-token classification is GPT-3 era; guided decoding and error-correcting decoders are decades old. What's new is the numbers. Nobody publishes negative results, so everyone relearns them.

September 2, 2026

2 September 2026: One city. One extraordinary sporting season. One destination. Melbourne is set for one of its biggest sporting seasons, with Crown Melbourne at the centre of the action. From Australia’s first regular NFL game to the Brownlow Medal, Group 1 racing, the Melbourne Cup Carnival and Australian Open Golf, the city’s sporting calendar will take centre stage this spring.

With the MCG preparing to host Australia’s first regular NFL season game on 11 September, Crown Melbourne will be the Official Home of Los Angeles Rams Fans in Australia and Official Fan Hotel, bringing fans together ahead of the historic game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers.

The Riverwalk is bringing the energy of the NFL to the heart of Southbank: transformed into a high-energy fan zone known as Rams House: The LA Tailgate Experience. Rams house is live from 10 September, giving the public the opportunity to experience the atmosphere of a Rams home game long into Saturday evening, featuring live music and entertainment, appearances from the Rams Cheerleaders and mascot, LA-style food trucks and merchandise stores. The match against the 49ers will be broadcast on a giant screen on a floating pontoon on the river.

On Saturday 12 September, Crown returns to Flemington Racecourse in 2026 as naming rights partner of the prestigious $750,000 Group 1 Crown Makybe Diva Stakes. We’ll also be back on the iconic Millionaire’s Row with the Crown marquee for Melbourne Cup Carnival, offering our signature party energy, striking design, elevated culinary experiences, and prime position overlooking the home straight.

The Crown Melbourne red carpet and Palladium will once again host the AFL Brownlow Medal, continuing a partnership spanning more than two decades, welcoming the biggest stars of the game and deciding who was best and fairest of them all ahead of the 2026 AFL Grand Final week.

THE LOCAL PROGRAM

State Treasurer Offers Low Interest Rate Loans to Local Government

State treasurer highlights impact of financing program during stop in Naches

Sept. 23, 2026

Washington State Treasurer Mike Pellicciotti stopped in Naches on Tuesday to look at a fire engine purchased with the help of his office. 

With the help of the LOCAL Program, Fire District 3 was able to finance half the cost of the fire engine. The program is a way for local governments to leverage the state's good credit to get low-interest financing for large purchases, like vehicles and real estate. 

Pellicciotti visit

A new fire engine sits in front of Naches Fire Department during a visit from Washington State Treasurer Mike Pellicciotti Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, in Naches, Wash.

"We've had nothing but success with the program," Pellicciotti said. "I can assure you it's the most favorable rate that any city is going to get."

The state is able to get much lower interest rates that cities would be able to find, Pellicciotti said. For Fire District 3, that interest rate was 1.9% on the $250,000 it needed to make the purchase.

The office offers the program three times a year. Participating local governments enter into a contract with the Office of the State Treasurer, which pools various agreements into Certificates of Participation, which are sold to investors similar to municipal bonds. 

Fire District 3 Chief Alan Baird said that the new fire truck replaced one from the 1990s. 

It was a busy season for his department of 30 volunteers. They cover around 300 acres of west Yakima County, including White Pass. There were a lot of mutual aid assists to fires in the Lower Valley, he said. 

The new truck was just one of several upgrades to his department, including new air packs for firefighters and a new brush truck.

text:
Norma Dumont vs. Ailín Pérez

Norma Dumont
At 35 years old (born October 1, 1990), the 5'7" orthodox fighter (67" reach, 38.5" leg reach) from Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil (originally Gordin Fight Team, later Syndicate MMA in Las Vegas under John Wood, with continued ties to Brazilian camps including Gordinho/CT Rules) enters with a pro record of 13-3. She has 2 submissions and 11 decisions. UFC record sits at 9-3.

Background and path: Father left when she was four. Started jiu-jitsu at 13, stopped to work as a secretary, then returned at 19 after a free Muay Thai class led her into Sanda. Six-time Minas Gerais Sanda state champion, Brazilian national Sanda champion, Sanda black belt, BJJ brown belt. Pro debut September 3, 2016 with a first round rear-naked choke of Tainara Lisboa. Went 4-0 regionally (Lisboa RNC, Patricia Borges Fernandes UD, Erica Leidianny Ribeiro RNC, Mariana Morais majority decision) before the UFC. Promotional debut was a first-round KO loss to Megan Anderson in February 2020. Rebounded with decisions over Ashlee Evans-Smith (missed weight at 139.5), Felicia Spencer (split), Aspen Ladd (five-round UD on short notice), then dropped a split to Macy Chiasson at catchweight after missing 145. Won five straight at featherweight/bantamweight over Danyelle Wolf, Karol Rosa, Chelsea Chandler, Germaine de Randamie, and Irene Aldana. Split decision over Ketlen Vieira in November 2025 was scored for Vieira by 6 of 7 media outlets. Joselyne Edwards snapped the run by unanimous decision in April 2026. Favorite weapons are the straight right, spinning back kick, harai goshi, and crossface.

Strengths: Range kickboxing from a Sanda base. Jab, calf/body kicks, straight right, front kicks, and occasional spinning attacks. Volume is there when she commits to it (159-69 significant strikes on Aldana, 3.85 SLpM career). 81% of her significant strikes come at distance. Durable chin after the debut KO and a long history of eating pressure without folding. Opportunistic wrestling when she chooses it with 6 takedowns on de Randamie, 3 on Chandler, trips and body-lock dumps that steal rounds. 72% takedown defense. Cardio to go 15 and 25 minutes. Composure on the bottom, she punched out of Vieira’s arm-triangle and survived de Randamie’s late armbar attempt.

Weaknesses: Zero career knockouts and zero UFC finishes. She wins rounds, she does not close them. Passive circling and single shot kicking let Edwards walk her down for 15 minutes (outstruck 70-51, 0-for-1 on takedowns). Macy Chiasson landed 6 takedowns on her and won a split. Two weight misses. Submission threat in the UFC is effectively zero. Ground striking is a small slice of her offense (6%). At 35 she is the older, higher-mileage fighter in a division that has already seen her fade into reactive kickboxing when pressured.

Ailín Pérez
At 31 years old (born October 5, 1994), the 5'5" switch-stance fighter (66" reach, 36" leg reach) from Zárate/Hurlingham, Buenos Aires, Argentina (trains at The Goat Shed Academy, lives and works out of the Miami area) enters with a pro record of 13-2. She has 4 KO/TKOs, 2 submissions, and 7 decisions. UFC record sits at 6-1.

Background and path: Started kung fu and Sanda at 11 or 12 because her brothers played rugby and she wanted a contact sport of her own. Red belt in kung fu, purple belt in BJJ, two-time South American Sanda champion (65kg and 70kg), two-time South American MMA bantamweight champion, Samurai Fight House champion. Fitness instructor before fighting paid enough. Amateur 1-0 (armbar). Pro debut November 24, 2018. Built the early record in Argentina/Uruguay (Galarza UD, Laura Ribeiro RNC for the CFU belt, Fiorella Cardozo TKO/retirement), then the 2021-22 Samurai Fight House run in Brazil/Argentina. Geyse Yasmin was a 30-25 style mauling of top control, crucifix GNP, slams, and stalled side control, Alessandra Tainara ate a trip to mount then a fight-ending head kick after breaking a clinch, Tamires Vidal was a messy clinch/wrestling fight Perez was winning before illegal knees to a downed opponent brought a R3 DQ and cost her the SFH belt, Romina Aguirre was an immediate body lock takedown, mount, and heavy elbows that cut her open for a R1 TKO, Stephanie Bragayrac was trips, heavy elbows, kimura attempts, and a corner stoppage after Pérez kicked the legs and piled on GNP. UFC debut was a R2 RNC loss to Stephanie Egger at featherweight. She has won six straight since dropping to 135: Evans-Smith (10 takedowns, 60-12 strikes, 30-25/30-25/30-26), Pudilová, Edwards, Zhelezniakova (arm-triangle at 3:52 of R1 after missing weight at 136.5), Rosa, Chiasson. Nickname “Fiona” is a Shrek joke. Favorite grappling technique is ground-and-pound. Single mother.

Strengths: Chain wrestling and top pressure at a rate almost nobody in the women’s bantamweight division matches. 4.90 takedowns per 15 minutes, 29 landed on 59 attempts in the UFC (49% accuracy), 73% takedown defense. Ten takedowns on Evans-Smith is tied for the most in a UFC women’s bout. Six each on Edwards and Chiasson. Body locks, outside trips, fence returns, slams. Once on top she is heavy: half guard, side control, mount, crucifix, shoulder pressure, elbows, and the arm-triangle that finished Zhelezniakova. Lowest significant strikes absorbed rate in UFC women’s bantamweight history (1.58 SApM). 35% of her significant strikes come on the ground. Spinning back fist is a weapon. It put Edwards on her seat. Regional finishing streak shows the same pattern the UFC decisions don't show. If the opponent cannot get up, the GNP gets ugly. Cardio to wrestle for 15 minutes. Mentally she forces ugly fights and is comfortable winning them 29-28.

Weaknesses: Standing output is low (2.88 SLpM) and the striking defense is only 57%. Rosa chewed the lead leg and won the third round clearly once the wrestling slowed. Edwards had her in a tight guillotine and swept her multiple times. Egger took the back and choked her. Referee stand-ups are a live problem because she will stall in side control (Yasmin, Chiasson, Rosa). Discipline issues are documented: DQ for illegal knees on Vidal, point/warning history, back of head strikes, a low blow sequence in that same Vidal fight. One UFC weight miss. She is the shorter, shorter-reach fighter and does not have a developed long range kicking game to keep a Sanda striker off her if the takedowns get stuffed. Most UFC wins are control time decisions, not damage decisions.

Stylistic Breakdown & Key Matchup Factors

Size & physicality: Dumont has the two-inch height edge and a one-inch reach edge. Perez is the stronger clinch wrestler. Neither is a big 135, but the frame advantage is Dumont’s and the chain-wrestling strength is Perez’s.

Striking: Dumont is the actual kickboxer. She can win a fight at range with the jab, calf kicks, body kicks, and straight right, and she already proved she can outland a pressure puncher for 15 minutes when she sits down on volume (Aldana). Perez’s standing game is entries, spinning back fists, the occasional head kick (Tainara), and dirty boxing into a shot. If this stays at kicking range for long stretches, Dumont should outland her similar to the way Edwards outlanded Dumont. Perez’s path is to make the pocket messy, spin, and close.

Grappling/Wrestling: This is the fight. Dumont’s 72% takedown defense did not hold up against Chiasson’s much lower-volume wrestling, and Edwards needed zero takedowns to beat Dumont because Dumont never imposed the grappling. When Dumont does wrestle first, she can win those minutes, de Randamie got dumped six times, Chandler three. The question is whether she will wrestle first against a better wrestler, or circle and kick the way she did against Edwards. Perez’s top game is control more than a constant submission hunt, but the arm-triangle is real and the GNP is heavier than Dumont’s. Dumont’s BJJ brown belt shows up as survival, not as a bottom player who sweeps at will. Edge to Perez in the wrestling exchanges and in the volume of attempts.

Pace & cardio: Both go 15 minutes as a habit. Dumont’s average fight time is 14:53 and Perez’s is 12:41, lowered by the Zhelezniakova finish and the Egger loss. Dumont has a five rounder on record. Perez’s pace is burst wrestling, stall, reset, burst-wrestle again. Dumont’s pace is measured kicking unless she is chasing a card, as she did in round 3 against Vieira. If Perez is forced to strike for three full rounds, the Rosa third round is the caution tape. If Dumont is forced to wrestle for three full rounds, the Chiasson fight is the caution tape.

Intangibles

Common opponents: Perez took Edwards down six times, knocked her down with a spinning back fist, and won a decision. Edwards then outstruck and walked down Dumont for a clean UD with almost no grappling. Chiasson landed six takedowns on Dumont and won a split, and Perez landed six on Chiasson and won a UD after dropping the first round. Both beat Karol Rosa by UD. Perez did it with two takedowns and a 62-53 strike edge, Dumont did it 35-33 and ate a knockdown. Both beat Ashlee Evans-Smith. Perez’s version was the 10-takedown rout.

The grudge?: Perez has asked for this since 2024. Dumont has said the fight was offered earlier and not taken. Brazil-Argentina, two years of “who ducked who,” and a fight that only got made after Dumont’s first loss in years.

Sanda childhood: Dumont kept the kickboxing. Perez kept the clinch, the trip, and the smash.

Mileage: Dumont has 12 UFC fights, a 25 minute main event, and is a week from 36. Perez has 7 UFC fights, a six fight streak, and is younger.

Wise Prediction

Perez will look to close the 5'7" frame immediately: body lock, fence, outside trip, mat return. She needs two or three completed takedowns a round and enough activity to keep ref stand-ups from erasing the control. If she gets mount or the far-side shoulder, the arm-triangle becomes live. Dumont will try to keep this at jab and calf kick range, stuff the first shot, and pile up the same kind of volume that buried Aldana.

Perez’s takedown rate, chain wrestling, and the common opponent tape (Edwards and Chiasson especially) give her the more reliable path. Dumont’s range striking, durability, and ability to steal a wrestling round when she actually shoots keep her live. This does not profile as a finish heavy fight. Dumont has never finished in the UFC. Perez’s last five UFC wins include one submission and four decisions.

My pick: Ailín Pérez by decision.

Why? The cleanest read on both records is that control time beats Dumont and range striking beats Perez. Perez is much better at forcing control time than Dumont is at forcing a 15-minute kickboxing match against someone who will not stay at kicking range. Chiasson already took Dumont down six times. Perez takes people down six times as a baseline. Dumont can win if she stuffs the entries and makes Perez box for three rounds, but that requires a defensive wrestling performance she has not shown against chain wrestlers, and an offensive striking performance she did not show against Edwards. Perez’s ugly, repeatable path is the one that keeps showing up.

Best bet angle: Primary lean is Perez on the moneyline. Perez by decision is the result. Over 2.5 rounds is the play. Dumont does not get finished, and Perez’s UFC finishes are one arm-triangle in seven fights. Perez by submission is the live method long shot if she mounts and finds the same arm-triangle. Dumont by decision is the most likely underdog result if the first three shots get stuffed and she wins a kicking fight. Dumont by KO/TKO is the thinnest method given 16 pro fights without a knockout.

text:
Always-On Agents: The Cost-Curve Rewrite and Privacy Paradox Behind Meta's Glasses Upgrade

Mark Zuckerberg released a key signal after Connect 2026: the AI experience on Meta($META ) glasses will shift within weeks from question-and-answer to a full-context always-on agent. Muse will run persistently in the background, hold complete context from everything the user has been discussing, and report back when work is done. Zuckerberg's exact words: users will be able to "talk with the full range of the voice capabilities that we just showed," and "it's gonna have the full context from everything that you've been discussing, and it's gonna be able to do work for you in the background."

This is not a feature update. This is a paradigm shift from voice remote control to ambient computing platform. The core tension behind that shift: the collision between always-on agent cost structure and privacy structure will determine whether Meta can transition from hardware subsidy model to subscription economy.

From 5-Second Delay to Always-On: The Quality Threshold

Understanding this upgrade requires understanding the prior experience defect. Current Meta glasses AI interaction is pull-based: the user says a wake word, the glasses capture a frame or a voice segment, upload to the cloud, and wait roughly five seconds for a response. Academic research has quantified the limitation: context-aware AI glasses that forward all queries to the cloud face approximately five-second query latency and roughly two hours of battery life.

Zuckerberg's new model is fundamentally different. Muse holds "the full context from everything you've been discussing." The glasses no longer wait for a user prompt to start the AI. They continuously maintain an ambient context buffer. When the user finally issues a request, Muse already holds sufficient context to deliver a coherent, history-grounded response instead of starting from zero.

Engadget confirmed the mechanism: users activate Muse by saying its name, and it "will work in the background and check in with you when it's finished." CNET reporters at Connect tested a Muse agent named "Henry," trained as "an assistant for a 38-year-old bodybuilding marketing executive," capable of giving dietary advice based on a Kind energy bar in front of the user and helping plan a workout.

That experience shift appears subtle but touches a fundamental architectural question: who bears the cost of maintaining always-on context?

Edge-Cloud Tiering: The Cost Curve Repricing

The answer sits in Meta's AI infrastructure architecture. According to AInvest, Meta glasses use a four-layer edge-AI architecture blending local processing and cloud inference. The financial logic: tasks handled locally generate almost no incremental AI inference cost for Meta.

Academic research provides more precise figures. When context-aware AI glasses forward all queries to the cloud, cloud cost is approximately $14 per frame per second. With edge-cloud tiering—sensing runs at the edge, invoking cloud models only when the scene changes—cloud cost drops to approximately $1.6 per hour, a 10-100x cost reduction. Battery life in context-aware AI use extends by at least 5x.

This means the always-on agent upgrade announced by Zuckerberg is financially feasible only if Meta has already prepared its edge-cloud tiering architecture. Muse's full-context capability does not mean all data goes to the cloud. Instead, the glasses maintain a local ambient context buffer and upload only compressed, filtered context fragments. Meta can keep the marginal inference cost of the always-on agent within an acceptable range.

But there is a variable that has not been fully priced: when Muse truly becomes an always-on service, what happens to user interaction frequency?

Under the current model, users must actively wake the AI, and each interaction generates one cloud inference call. Under the always-on model, Muse works continuously in the background, "checking in when it's finished." If frequency jumps from a few times per day to dozens, total inference costs may rise significantly even if per-call cost declines due to edge tiering.

Muse's pricing structure suggests Meta anticipated this risk. The free tier provides 100 million tokens per week. Paid tiers at $20/month provide 500 million tokens and $100/month provides 3 billion tokens. Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang stated "for the vast majority of users, they should be able to do what they need to within the free tier." The design logic: offer the always-on agent as part of the hardware experience for free, but direct heavy usage—especially complex task chains and extended background operations—toward paid tiers.

The Privacy Paradox: The Sharpest Competitive Barrier

If the always-on agent is the functional leap, privacy is the structural risk. And the nature of this risk is more complex than it appears.

Financial Times reporting revealed a key fact: Meta is developing "Super Sensing" prototype glasses capable of continuous audio recording and photo capture every few seconds. More critically, executives "currently plan to not activate the LED indicator when super-sensing features are running." Meta's rationale in a 2025 policy document: "If the LED blinks for a long time—say, every time there's an AI interaction—people might stop noticing it, reducing awareness that photos or videos are being captured."

That rationale is logically coherent but legally fragile. Fox Rothschild's chief AI and information security officer Mark McCreary noted: "A dozen-plus states require all parties to consent before a private conversation is recorded, so a device capturing audio without an indicator light is a walking consent problem, not just a design quirk." Between 11 and 13 states require two-party consent to record a conversation, making the legal risk of always-on audio capture far exceed Meta's current compliance framework.

But the privacy issue's impact on Meta's business model extends beyond legal risk. CNET reporters at Connect put it bluntly: "If you were worried about AI on devices many call 'spy glasses' before, they're about to be supercharged." This public sentiment is forming a market entry barrier—not a technology barrier, but a social acceptance barrier. German data protection authorities have confirmed that Meta glasses' LED indicator "is not easily visible in many environments, particularly outdoors and in direct sunlight," and Hamburg's data protection commissioner has announced intent to ban the use of Meta smart glasses in public spaces. The European Data Protection Board's report on the smart glasses category is due within weeks.

Apple's strategy precisely exploits this barrier. Apple's N50 smart glasses have been delayed to a June 2027 WWDC reveal, with Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reporting the delay is directly related to privacy concerns. Apple is evaluating a middle-ground design: "keep cameras but prevent them from capturing photos or videos, using them only to feed visual data into AI tools that identify objects and places." Apple's privacy features include on-device AI processing, no cloud video uploads or human review, tamper-proof camera indicators, and blocking the use of customer recordings to train AI models.

This creates a clear competitive dynamic. Meta pursues functional leadership: richer AI experiences, deeper context understanding, more proactive agent behavior. Apple pursues trust leadership: stricter privacy protection, clearer user consent mechanisms, more conservative data processing. The outcome depends not on technical parameters but on how much privacy users will sacrifice for how much function.

The Scale Constraint on Subscription Revenue: A Calibration Needed

Muse's paid tier pricing—$20/month and $100/month—represents Meta's first direct charge to consumers for AI services. But Meta's financial reality requires calibrating expectations for this revenue's scale.

Meta's Q2 2026 total revenue was $60.8 billion, with advertising revenue accounting for approximately 98%. Even if Muse achieves high conversion among smart glasses users, the absolute scale of subscription revenue remains a rounding error relative to advertising revenue. Jefferies modeled a long-term scenario: 1 billion users, 3% paid conversion rate, approximately $10.8 billion in annual revenue. That figure needs to be placed against Meta's $60.8 billion quarterly revenue—less than two quarters of advertising revenue.

A more conservative estimate. Counterpoint Research reports global AI glasses shipments rose 263% year-on-year in H1 2026, with display-less AI glasses accounting for 96% of total shipments and Meta holding 94% share of that segment, with volumes up 260% year-on-year and 22% sequentially. IDC places Meta at 68.7% of overall smart glasses shipments. Assuming Meta glasses cumulative active user base reaches 15-20 million units by end-2026, even at a 10% conversion rate to the $20/month tier, annual subscription revenue would be roughly $360-480 million. At 20% conversion, roughly $720 million to $960 million.

These figures remain small relative to Reality Labs' annual operating loss (Q2 2026 alone was $4.62 billion on $431 million revenue, annualizing to roughly $18.5 billion in losses on $1.7 billion in revenue). But the significance of subscription revenue is not its absolute scale but its marginal contribution rate. Once edge-cloud tiering keeps marginal inference costs low, the incremental margin on subscription revenue will be far higher than advertising revenue. This is Meta's first quantifiable anchor in the transition from attention economy to utility economy.

A Verifiable Tracking Framework

For investors and analysts tracking Meta's glasses AI strategy, the following indicators matter more than product launches for reflecting the business's true health:

Muse weekly active users and daily interaction counts on glasses. This determines the actual load on the edge-cloud tiering architecture. If daily interactions exceed design thresholds, inference costs may exceed expectations.

Conversion rates between free and paid tiers. Jefferies modeled a 3% long-term paid conversion rate. Helfstein's framework benchmarks against ChatGPT's ~6% free-to-paid rate. No public data currently exists. If conversion falls below 5%, the strategic significance of subscription revenue needs reassessment.

The number of privacy-related complaints, regulatory investigations, and media reports involving Meta glasses. German data protection authorities have confirmed LED indicator visibility issues outdoors, and Hamburg has announced intent to ban public use. This is a real-time indicator of the social acceptance barrier.

EssilorLuxottica wearable gross margin quarterly trajectory. H1 2026 adjusted gross margin reached 63.5%, up 10 basis points year-on-year, with AI glasses profitability improvement as a key driver. If the always-on agent upgrade pushes volume growth but gross margin comes under pressure again, scale economics on the hardware side have not yet formed.

Apple N50 final product specifications, especially camera strategy. If Apple chooses a camera-less design, Meta's functional leadership advantage widens further. If Apple finds a middle path balancing privacy and visual intelligence, Meta's competitive window narrows.

Zuckerberg's upgrade announcement is essentially Meta betting on one thing: users' perceived utility of an always-on AI agent will exceed their privacy erosion concerns. This is an unverified hypothesis. And the cost of verifying it—whether through market feedback or regulatory action—is being absorbed in Reality Labs' quarterly losses exceeding $4 billion.

text:
I started listing the ways a person can place a bet now and I could not finish the list.

Sportsbook on the phone. Casino floor. Horse track. Slots in a gas station in some states. Scratch tickets at the register. Loot boxes in a game nobody calls gambling. Crypto whatever. And now the prediction markets, where you can put money on an election, which is a sentence that would have sounded insane fifteen years ago and sounds like a tuesday now.

There is no edge of it anymore. That is what got my attention. It used to have edges.

Here are the actual numbers, because they are public and they are better than any argument I could make up.

In 2025 the regulated sportsbooks in this country took in about 165 billion dollars in wagers. They kept about 16.8 billion of it. That is a hold rate of roughly ten percent. Thirty nine states plus DC and Puerto Rico have legal sports betting now. Over eighty percent of it happens on a phone. Two companies, FanDuel and DraftKings, run about eighty percent of the online market between them.

Ten percent. Printed. Published. Not hidden, not a conspiracy, not a rumor. For every dollar that moves through, the house keeps about a dime, and everybody involved can look that number up in about nine seconds.

And here is the thing nobody says plainly about that number. A ten percent hold means the business does not need you to lose. It needs you to play. The book does not care which side wins any particular game, because it is not gambling, it is collecting. The product being sold is not the bet. It is the frequency of the bet.

Which explains every feature that has shown up in the last few years. Parlays. Same game parlays. Live betting where you can wager on the next pitch. Bonus bets that expire. None of that improves your odds. All of it increases how often you are in.

But the real change was not the odds and it was not human weakness either, and this is the part I keep coming back to.

It was the drive.

Gambling used to require going somewhere. A casino was a building. For most of this country it was a building in another state, which meant a plane ticket or six hours in a car, a hotel, a decision made on a monday about a weekend. Nobody designed that as a safety feature. It was just friction, sitting there by accident, doing an enormous amount of work.

The drive was a cooling off period. You had to still want it at hour four.

Now it is a thumb. The distance between the impulse and the money leaving is under a second, at two in the morning, in bed, while the game is still going. Nothing was added to make people weaker. Something was removed that had been quietly protecting them, and the removal got sold as convenience.

The research caught up to this and it is not subtle.

The New York Fed found credit delinquencies rose about three tenths of a percent across states that legalized. Small, until you look at the roughly three percent of the population who actually bet, where delinquencies jumped more than ten percent. Young adults took the worst of it, steepest under forty. A UCLA study by Brett Hollenbeck found average credit scores down about eight tenths of a point statewide, and in states with online betting specifically, a ten percent increase in the likelihood of bankruptcy and an eight percent rise in debt sent to collections. Both effects showing up roughly two years after legalization, which is about how long it takes for the friction to finish disappearing.

Average quarterly spend by bettors went from under five hundred dollars at the end of 2019 to over a thousand by the middle of 2021.

Now let me be fair about what those numbers actually say, because they cut both ways and I am not going to use only the half I like.

Most people who bet are fine. That three percent figure matters. The overwhelming majority place twenty dollars on a game, lose it, laugh, and go to work monday with their life entirely intact. That is a real thing and it is most of the activity. Anybody telling you gambling is destroying everybody is selling something too.

But look at what it means that the damage concentrates. If the harm sits in a small slice, and the revenue is enormous, then a meaningful share of that revenue is coming from people who are in trouble. Not all of it. A share. And every product decision aimed at increasing frequency lands hardest on exactly the people who least needed another opportunity.

The political betting is its own strange thing and I have not decided how I feel.

One company doing it was valued around eleven billion dollars last november after raising a billion. Congress spent this spring asking the regulators what exactly is happening over there. And put the regulation aside for a second and look at the object itself. A market where you can profit from a result that makes your own neighbors worse off. There is something genuinely new in being paid to be correct about other people's trouble, and I do not think we have language for it yet.

Two minds, real ones.

One side of me says adults get to do what they want with their own money. I do not want a country where somebody decides which of my enjoyments is approved. The cure is usually worse, the enforcement always lands on ordinary people, and a man who wants to put forty dollars on a football game has not wronged anybody.

The other side says consent means something different when one party has the data and the other has a feeling. These interfaces were built by people who know precisely which color and which notification and which hour produces another wager. Agreeing to that is not the same as choosing it. It is closer to being outplayed.

I do not resolve that and I would be lying if I said I did.

What I do believe is smaller. Watch yourself honestly. Not in a dramatic way, just notice. Notice if the fun stopped being fun and turned into getting it back. Notice if it is a thing you do or a thing you hide. The lying starts before the losing gets bad, every time, and it usually starts with lying to yourself first.

Because when somebody goes down this way, they do not go alone. That is the part that actually gets me. The people closest to them absorb it without ever having placed a bet. They did not consent to anything, they just live there. That is where most of the real damage sits, and it never shows up in a single statistic anybody publishes.

And people do come back from this. Not easily, not quickly, but they do, and a man in the hole should know the hole has a way out of it rather than assuming it does not.

As for me, I have no idea what I am on about here and no policy to offer anybody. Two cents, freely given, worth about that. I just feel for the folks who lost themselves in it, and I am not convinced most of them ever saw the moment it stopped being a game.

-Zekie

But they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction and perdition.

1 Timothy 6:9

text:
South-pole parking spots: Isaacman’s “good deals” doctrine

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman just said the quiet part about lunar real estate. In Ars Technica’s Sep 22 report on his Air & Space Forces Association remarks, he compared the Moon’s surface to Africa and the south pole’s useful real estate to Washington, D.C.—only so many roads, only so many good parking spots. The spots that matter combine permanently shadowed crater floors holding water ice with nearby ridges that catch near-continuous sunlight for power. Those are the same ridges China is targeting with Russia as a partner, Isaacman warned, including the prospect of a fission reactor on the surface that could deny the United States a training environment it needs for Mars.

That geography lesson is procurement policy in disguise. Isaacman said the White House instruction is simple: only “good deals.” Italy’s more-than-$5-billion commitment to a lunar habitat module—and two Italian astronauts on the surface—is the example he likes. Japan’s multibillion-dollar pressurized rover, also trading for two crewed seats, is the other. Flag collections and late robotic landers that arrive after the ridges are claimed get a cold reception; he dismissed a partner offer of a mid-2030s Shackleton lander while China prepares Chang’e-7 for early 2027. The likely target of that critique is ESA’s Argonaut-class cargo concept, which overlaps capabilities Blue Origin’s Blue Moon and SpaceX’s Starship landers already plan to sell.

Why Orbital treats this as a Wednesday story, not a quote farm: Artemis Accords signatures and Gateway cancellations only make sense if you map them onto ice, power, and timelines. Gateway’s scrub left ESA and Canada scrambling to redefine contributions after astronaut seats had been priced against orbital modules. Italy negotiating a habitat outside ESA’s committee pace is a feature of Isaacman’s doctrine, not a bug. Meaningful contributions accelerate the mission; committee drag does not.

NASA Goddard’s Artemis south-pole science explainer is the clean YouTube companion; Ars is the dated web primary. Watch whether ESA locks a surface role that is additive rather than competitive with US industry, whether Canada finds a partial-gravity robotics niche, and whether Chang’e-7’s slip or success resets the urgency rhetoric. Orbital’s scoreboard is not applause lines. It is signed hardware on a calendar that still beats a rival to the ridge.

Nuclear wording stays precise here: Isaacman referred to a Chinese surface reactor concept—fission power—not a Pu-238 RTG. Those are different machines and should never be conflated in paste copy.

For operators and allies, the message is transactional in the useful sense. Bring a habitat, a rover, or another gap-filler NASA has not already bought from US firms, and seats follow. Bring a press release and a mid-2030s PowerPoint, and the parking spots will be taken. South-pole ice made the Moon a real-estate fight. Isaacman just published the lease terms.

More than you might think.

CRINK FAULT LINE WIDENS: MOSCOW, BEIJING AND TEHRAN PULL IN DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS

A significant policy divergence is becoming visible inside the China–Russia–Iran relationship.

On 22 September, Vladimir Putin and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called for safe and unimpeded passage through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, alongside rapid de-escalation in Yemen. The Kremlin said a political and diplomatic settlement remained the preferred course. (Reuters⁠)

Iran’s position is different.

Tehran has offered to reopen Hormuz only if Washington reduces military pressure and ends restrictions affecting Iranian ports. At the UN on 23 September, President Masoud Pezeshkian reinforced the principle behind that position: Iran would not permit other states unrestricted benefit from Hormuz while the waterway could simultaneously be used against Iranian interests. (Reuters⁠)

That creates a clear strategic contradiction:

>Russia wants predictable maritime trade.
>China needs secure energy routes.
>Iran is retaining Hormuz as negotiating leverage.

There is another potentially important signal. Reuters reported that Beijing has discussed using pressure on Iran as part of negotiations with Washington over Taiwan-related issues. That remains reported diplomacy - not evidence China has abandoned Tehran - but it illustrates how Chinese interests can diverge sharply from Iranian ones. 

Truth Desk assessment: CRINK remains a partnership of overlapping interests, not a unified alliance. The emerging vulnerability is increasingly obvious: when national interests collide, solidarity has limits.

text:
PALO ALTO NETWORKS $PANW BUILT A PRODUCT ON THE AI THAT KNOCKED IT DOWN 6% IN MARCH. TODAY IT LED THE S&P 500:

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) at $392.50 (after hours), +$17.93 / +4.79% today, after a regular close of $393.30, up 5.0% - the biggest gain in the S&P 500, which closed at 7,706.03, -58.61 / -0.75%. The Santa Clara, California company sells software that keeps attackers out of corporate networks. It added about $15B of market value on a day the 10-year Treasury yield - what Washington pays to borrow for ten years - closed near 5.11%, up about 0.15 point, its highest since 2007, and pulled down most stocks priced on future growth.

The verdict: Palo Alto now trades as the market's bet on how dangerous AI is getting. Its two biggest gains this year came on other companies' news, and its biggest drop followed its own strong report. Today fits that pattern, so the price is tracking a theme first and the company's numbers second.

The news came a day early. On Tuesday morning Palo Alto launched Unit 42 Continuous Frontier AI Defense, a service that probes a client's own systems around the clock for weak spots before criminals find them. It runs on AI models built to find software holes, including Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Cyber; both private labs share them only with vetted partners. Palo Alto says it found a year's worth of weak spots inside its own company in three weeks, and some at every client tested, 37% rated high or critical.

The stock rose 0.8% Tuesday. The 5% came Wednesday, with the other security stocks:

- CrowdStrike (CRWD) at $261.09 (after hours), +$11.03 / +4.41% today, after touching a record $263.19
- First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR), a fund of security stocks, at $104.35 (after hours), +$1.78 / +1.73%

The case buyers made: security budgets survive slowdowns, and every new AI tool is one more door to guard. CrowdStrike, which protects laptops and cloud accounts, fits none of the six Len5es: at over 7,000 times its past year's profit, it offers no earnings for the value or growth styles to weigh.

That theme has steered the stock all year:

- February 24: a one-year low, $139.57, a week after its own report and days after Anthropic unveiled an AI tool that scans code for security holes
- March 27: -6.0%, on a leaked Anthropic draft warning that Mythos-class models could exploit software holes faster than defenders respond
- April 7: +4.9%, when Anthropic shared an early Mythos with a select group of companies, Palo Alto included
- August 27: +12.8%, on CrowdStrike's better-than-expected quarterly report
- September 2: -9.3%, the day after Palo Alto's own report beat forecasts
- September 14: +13.1%, after Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman publicly warned about AI's risks

The same model went from the reason to sell to the thing Palo Alto sells. The stock is up 113% this year and 2.8 times its February low. The lesson in that list: when a stock swings harder on its industry's headlines than on its own reports, its price is carrying a story, and a story can fade faster than revenue.

Underneath, the September 1 report:

- Revenue $3.41B in the July quarter, +34%; $11.48B for the year to July 31, +24%
- Next-Generation Security ARR - the yearly value of its newer subscription products - $9.10B, +63%
- Free cash flow - cash left after running the business and buying equipment - $4.11B for the year, about 36 cents per sales dollar
- Standard-accounting net loss $282M in the July quarter, vs a $254M profit a year earlier; the $1.02 adjusted profit per share excludes stock pay and CyberArk deal costs

That 63% is partly bought. CyberArk, which guards logins and passwords, and Chronosphere, which monitors cloud software, both joined during the year. In the April quarter they supplied $1.6B of the $8.1B subscription total; the rest grew about 28%. For the year to July 2027, with both deals counted in both years, Palo Alto forecasts 22%-23%.

The strongest fact for the stock: customers are signing. The July quarter added nearly $1B of new subscription value, and contracted revenue not yet booked reached $21.2B, +34%. Chief executive Nikesh Arora said on the report's call that every CEO now wants to test their company against Mythos.

The strongest fact against it: the price. At $392.50, Palo Alto costs about 94 times the $4.16-$4.19 of adjusted profit per share it forecasts for the year to July 2027.

VERDICT: a fast-growing, cash-rich business whose stock now moves on AI headlines, priced as if those headlines keep turning into customers. Palo Alto sits on none of the six Len5es. The nearest is Momentum, which hunts a price near its one-year high with short and long climbs agreeing: the long climb is there, but today was only its first close above its pre-report $382.13, still 1.6% under the $398.88 August 13 high. What would put Palo Alto on the Momentum Len5: a close above $398.88 that holds. At 94 times forecast profit, the value Len5es are out on price. Losses in the last two quarters keep it off the Quality Len5; a return to standard-accounting profit as CyberArk costs fade would put it on the Quality Len5.

WHEN: fiscal first-quarter results, tentatively November 18 after the close, not yet confirmed by Palo Alto. Its own forecast: revenue $3.30B-$3.31B, adjusted profit $0.96-$0.98 a share. The number that decides it: Next-Generation Security ARR against its $9.54B-$9.56B forecast. RISK: a quiet stretch for AI headlines, which have moved this stock as much as its reports.

In February the market sold Palo Alto because AI might do a defender's job. Today it bought the stock because AI makes that job bigger. November 18 is the first report that has to show which of those customers are paying for.

Game On

September 2, 2026

2 September 2026: One city. One extraordinary sporting season. One destination. Melbourne is set for one of its biggest sporting seasons, with Crown Melbourne at the centre of the action. From Australia’s first regular NFL game to the Brownlow Medal, Group 1 racing, the Melbourne Cup Carnival and Australian Open Golf, the city’s sporting calendar will take centre stage this spring.

With the MCG preparing to host Australia’s first regular NFL season game on 11 September, Crown Melbourne will be the Official Home of Los Angeles Rams Fans in Australia and Official Fan Hotel, bringing fans together ahead of the historic game between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers.

The Riverwalk is bringing the energy of the NFL to the heart of Southbank: transformed into a high-energy fan zone known as Rams House: The LA Tailgate Experience. Rams house is live from 10 September, giving the public the opportunity to experience the atmosphere of a Rams home game long into Saturday evening, featuring live music and entertainment, appearances from the Rams Cheerleaders and mascot, LA-style food trucks and merchandise stores. The match against the 49ers will be broadcast on a giant screen on a floating pontoon on the river.

On Saturday 12 September, Crown returns to Flemington Racecourse in 2026 as naming rights partner of the prestigious $750,000 Group 1 Crown Makybe Diva Stakes. We’ll also be back on the iconic Millionaire’s Row with the Crown marquee for Melbourne Cup Carnival, offering our signature party energy, striking design, elevated culinary experiences, and prime position overlooking the home straight.

The Crown Melbourne red carpet and Palladium will once again host the AFL Brownlow Medal, continuing a partnership spanning more than two decades, welcoming the biggest stars of the game and deciding who was best and fairest of them all ahead of the 2026 AFL Grand Final week.

From 1 October to 10 November, Racing Victoria’s immersive celebration of Victorian racing will fill Crown’s Atrium, featuring fashion, racing memorabilia, interactive storytelling, and racing legend tributes including Phar Lap, marking 100 years since the champion’s birth.

The 2026 golf Australian Open will then return to the Melbourne Sandbelt in December with Crown the major partner and home away from home for the world’s biggest golf stars, including returning green jacket headliner, Rory McIlroy.

As the city welcomes thousands of visitors for a season expected to deliver significant tourism and economic activity, Crown will activate across every major sporting code, offering exclusive fan experiences, iconic events, and world-class hospitality all under one roof.

Crown Melbourne CEO, Ed Domingo, said: “No other city on earth lives and breathes sport the way Melbourne does, and Crown is proud to play a leading role in bringing its biggest moments to life. This spring, major sporting events will put Melbourne firmly in the global spotlight and drive real impact across tourism, hospitality and the visitor economy. From the NFL and the Brownlow Medal to Group 1 racing and the Melbourne Cup Carnival, Crown will be where fans, visitors and locals come together to experience the energy of the city at its best.” (Source: Crown Resorts)

Casino (1995) – Martin Scorsese Film & Its Informal "Series"

The iconic 1995 film Casino directed by Martin Scorsese, starring Robert De Niro, Joe Pesci, and Sharon Stone, is often grouped with Scorsese’s other mafia/gangster films as an unofficial trilogy:

Goodfellas (1990)
Casino (1995)
The Irishman (2019)

Fans and critics frequently refer to these three as Scorsese’s “Casino trilogy” or “mob series,” even though they are not direct sequels.

text:
Most business owners will charge the exact same rate in 2027 that they charged in 2026.

That is not loyalty. 
That is a slow-motion pay cut.

Your cost of living went up. 
Your software stack went up. 
Your skills went up. 
Your price stayed flat.

Here is the discipline I run every single year, and what I coach my clients to run:

→ 30 to 60 days before the new year, you send the notice. Not on January 1. Before. 
→ The message is simple: it has been great working with you this year, we reassess our rates annually, here is the new rate moving forward, happy to answer any questions. 
→ If the results have been there, they will not fight you. If they push back, everything is negotiable except taxes and death. Bring your talking points.

New skills earn a new price. 
That is not arrogance, it is math.

But raising rates only works if the foundation is set. Two things have to be true first:

1. Your offer has to be validated. Paid ads scale what already converts. If nothing is converting, ads just burn the budget faster. Crawl, walk, then run.

2. Your ICP has to be surgical. Not "small businesses." Try this instead: physical therapy and chiropractic offices, Southern California, $2M in revenue, 10+ employees, multiple locations. That level of clarity is what turns NOs into YESes.

Visibility + Credibility = Profitability. You need both. Most people only have a visibility problem, and they think it is a pricing problem.

25+ years, $100M+ in trackable revenue, 200+ businesses. The ones who grow every year are the ones who raise rates every year.

When did YOU last raise yours?

✨Work Wednesday is a weekly staff spotlight series from the California Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation that highlights the people behind California’s climate, equity, and community development work.

As we celebrate Latino Heritage Month, we’re recognizing the histories, cultures, achievements and contributions of Latino communities that have helped shape California for generations.

This week, we introduce you to Eric De La Cruz, the Executive Director of the Racial Equity Commission. Eric speaks on how his grandparent's legacy of justice for the Mexican-American community set the foundation for him to fight for injustices everywhere.

Each episode features a member of our team sharing their role, current projects, and the impact of their work across the state. text:
One April turn reveals Mammoth’s best skiing window

At Mammoth Mountain above Mammoth Lakes, California, skiers dropping beneath Chair 23 found fresh tracks when much of ski country was already winding down.

The first skier’s turn changed my answer. I used to treat April as the month you accepted whatever winter had left. Here, the mountain can still deliver powder-then offer soft spring snow once the sun takes over.

Mammoth’s 11,053-foot summit helps explain that contrast. The resort averages about 400 inches of snow a season, while its long, bright spring days create a useful freeze-and-thaw cycle: firm early snow gradually softens into forgiving turns.

That is why I would choose April, especially for confident skiers who enjoy adjusting their timing. Start on slopes that soften first, then move higher as the sun reaches them. The Chair 23 group waited for access and was rewarded with clean powder, but those untouched lines disappeared quickly.

The trade-off is real. Wind can delay the upper lifts, mornings may feel hard, and operations begin concentrating around Main Lodge after mid-April. Historical snowfall is evidence of possibility, never a promise.

Still, April balances deep coverage, longer light, spring events and better-value offers better than any other Mammoth window for me. It rewards the skier who watches the mountain instead of demanding one kind of snow all https://t.co/SsUzDxnvnn

text:
Retirement anxiety is rarely about net worth. It is almost always about cash-flow plumbing.

Cerulli survey data shows 40% of all retirees report moderate-to-severe financial stress.

For retirees with a documented wealth plan, that drops to 29%. (Since the 40% includes planners, the unguided cohort is even higher).

Look at what actually drives the anxiety:

1.) Inflation: 21% (August CPI at 3.4%)

2.) Healthcare costs: 16% (Medicare Part B rose 9.7% this year)

3.) Economic downturn: 14%

Market drawdowns rank last. The real fear is non-discretionary purchasing power getting eaten alive.

When investors lack a cash-flow framework, every market dip feels like a threat to their lifestyle. They panic-sell risk assets at the bottom to fund next month's cash needs, crystallizing sequence-of-returns risk.

Proper portfolio architecture solves this mechanically: 

• Ring-fence 2–3 years of distributions in contractual yield and short-duration cash proxies. 

• Let equity beta compound uninhibited without lifestyle liquidation drag. 

• Deploy real assets and private credit to outpace non-discretionary cost inflation.

You can't control inflation prints or equity pullbacks. But with an asset-liability matching framework, market volatility never forces you to liquidate capital at the wrong time.

A plan isn't a static document. It’s liquidity insurance for your balance sheet.

Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes has been approved to move to a halfway house next year, SWR News reported – the latest development after a stunning downfall that culminated in a conviction for defrauding investors while running her failed blood testing startup.

She is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, in August 2027, SWR News reported, citing an update from the Department of Justice’s Victim Notification System.

Holmes was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison in 2022 after she was convicted on multiple charges of conspiracy to defraud investors and wire fraud related to the now-defunct company. Her sentence has since been reduced by a year.

Holmes is currently being held at Federal Prison Camp Bryan in southern Texas, a minimum security federal prison camp that is approximately 100 miles from Houston, where she grew up before moving to California to attend Stanford.

Holmes was once an icon in the tech world, serving as a poster child for the limitless ambitions and potential of Silicon Valley. Her company began to unravel after a Wall Street Journal investigation in 2015 reported that Theranos had only ever performed roughly a dozen of the hundreds of tests it offered using its proprietary technology, and with questionable accuracy. It also came to light that Theranos was relying on third-party manufactured devices from traditional blood testing companies rather than its own technology. Theranos ultimately dissolved in September 2018.

The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to provide information on the move, saying it doesn’t discuss “the conditions of confinement for any individual, including release plans.”

“BOP assigns individuals to facilities based on several factors. These include the level of security and supervision required, medical or programmatic needs, separation or security considerations necessary for the individual’s safety, and other relevant factors, such as proximity to the individual’s release residence,” the spokesperson told SWR Wednesday.

Halfway houses, also known as residential reentry centers, offer a supervised environment for inmates nearing release and services including career counseling and financial management assistance, according to the bureau.

The Austin Transitional Center is a 460-bed “community corrections center” owned by a private prison company. It’s located about 7 miles southeast of downtown Austin and is one of eight residential reentry centers in Texas.
