MANUSCRIPT:
Series:   “Daniel: God’s Sovereign Plans” #34 
Text:   Daniel 12:1–3
By:   Shaun Marksbury     
Date:   September 13, 2026
Venue:   Living Water Baptist Church  
Occasion:   PM Service

Introduction
The doctrine of the last things should be an encouragement to us.  As we’ve previously noted, though, too often it is not.  People grow fearful in their speculations as dates are set and predictions made that are later quietly abandoned.  Rumors fill the gaps where God has not revealed.  Even so, God has revealed what He did so His people have hope and comfort.

We see that hope in this concluding chapter the Book of Daniel.  It provides additional insight into the tribulation and more.  We see that this occurs “at that time,” which is “the end time” according to 11:40.[1]  This is continuing the same vision from chapter 10 through 11, so that makes sense.

Those who are facing the horrors of this time can know that there is a message of hope for those who die in persecution.  Daniel, who had lived to see so much, likewise wants this hope.  To keep it simple, we’ll just consider three aspects of the end times and the hope it brings.  First, the crisis of the end times (v. 1).  Second, the resurrections of the end times (v. 2).  Third, the glory of the end times (v. 3).

First, the Crisis of the End Times (v. 1)
Now at that time, Michael, the great prince who stands guard over the sons of your people, will stand. And there will be a time of distress such as never happened since there was a nation until that time; and at that time your people, everyone who is found written in the book, will be rescued.

This is an unparalleled distress, a severe trial upon the earth as we considered in the past two messages.  Nothing in human history fully describes it.  Yet, even here, there is good news, for the text immediately introduces Michael.  This means that, while the worst suffering imaginable is happening, it isn’t without divine protection.

Again, this is continuing the career of the final wicked king who began a policy of persecution.  This will include a war against the Jewish people in particular.[2]  We are seeing, even today, a time when the world is turning more antisemitic, and that may well help set the stage for these events.

Remember, this is a passage addressed to Daniel’s people.  We saw this earlier in the 70 Weeks prophecy, where we saw that the weeks were decreed “for your people and your holy city” (9:24).  In this prophecy, we’ve seen all through chapter 11 that the historical focus has been on Israel.  And, lest we forget, most of the book of Daniel takes place within the Babylonian Captivity.  This is a Jewish-centric book, and so, when we read about a defense here for “your people,” we are reading about the Jewish people.

The Lord reveals defense for them through Michael the archangel, who we saw back in 10:13 and 21.  Some think he is Christ, but there is no biblical reason to believe that.  Christ is, of course, the chief protector of His people, but He can certainly charge and send forth a prince of His angels to accomplish the task (and “prince” can refer to angels[3]).  As MacArthur notes here, Michael “ministers with special attention to protecting Israel during that Gentile time (cf. Is. 26:20, 21; Jer. 30:7; Matt. 24:21).”[4]  The Lord directs His prince to protect the Jewish people.

We’ve already seen part of the reason why they need protection.  Michael’s involvement will give the people of Israel hope that they will not entirely perish in the successful campaigns of the Antichrist.  Moreover, there seems to be some kind of spiritual protection taking place, as Revelation 12 discusses.  In that vision, we read about a dragon attacking a woman who is a symbol for the people of Israel.  After her Son is caught up, the dragon attacks her.

A battle then takes place in heaven.  This is during the last half of the Tribulation, and it’s lead by Michael against Satan and his forces (cf. Dan. 12:7; 12:11–12).  Michael and his angels defeat Satan’s forces at this time so decisively that they lose their place in heaven.  These heavenly and the earthly realities are more linked than we understand, because what happens in heaven shapes what happens on earth, as we see in three ways.

First, this battle will result in the ultimate shift in cosmic authority.  In Revelation 12:10, a heavenly voice announces that salvation, power, and God’s kingdom have arrived because Satan the accuser has been hurled down to earth.  Thus, he can no longer fulfill his role as the prosecuting voice against believers before God’s throne day and night and permanently loses access to heaven.  Even the brethren today should be looking forward to this!

Second, Michael’s victory becomes the basis for earthly triumph.  As G. K. Beale notes, “When there is conflict between the saints and the world on earth, there is corresponding conflict in the heavenly dimension.”[5]  Inversely, because Michael will conquer Satan’s forces in heaven and cast them out, believers on earth will more powerfully overcome Satan through the blood of the Lamb and their testimony (v. 11).

Third, and unfortunately, Satan’s expulsion intensifies earthly opposition (vv. 13, 15, 17).  He will focus on destroying Israel before his eventual defeat at Armageddon.  As Revelation 12:12 says, “For this reason, rejoice, O heavens and you who dwell in them.  Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time.” He will try to do as much damage as possible to the people of God as possible before he meets his end.

Remember, though, that Michael will be protecting Israel on earth.  We see protection in Revelation 12.  When the devil focuses on Israel, the people are delivered safely as on a great eagle to a wilderness place (v. 14).  When the devil then unleashes a torrential attack that might have swept away others, earth opens its mouth and swallows the flood (v. 16).  It’s clear that Michael’s involvement provides significant protection for Israel throughout the remaining 3 ½ years of the tribulation.

Now, you might wonder about Gentile believers, but remember, this is the end of the “times of the Gentiles.”  Gentiles who come to Christ will benefit from Michael’s activities, but they are not the focus of them.  As the text says here, “And there will be a time of distress such as never occurred since there was a nation until that time.”  The term for “distress” in the Greek translation of this verse is the same Jesus uses in Matthew 24:21 — “For then there will be a great tribulation, such as has not occurred since the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will.”[6]  As we see in Revelation 12:17, the great dragon will eventually focus on those believers who are not under Michael’s direct protection, unfortunately.  This is a serious time for everyone upon the earth.

It will also be, as Jeremiah called it, “the time of Jacob’s distress” (Jer. 30:7).  Nothing in the persecutions under Antiochus IV Epiphanes, as severe as they were, exhausts this language.  As such, Michael’s actions are needed in redeeming the Jewish people, though, both physically and also spiritually as they repent and trust in the Messiah.  As one author notes, “God will keep His covenant with Abraham and see to it that the Jewish remnant will enter into their promised kingdom.”[7]  Thankfully, the elect will be delivered, one way or the other.

Now, this obviously includes Gentile Christians, but the focus is more upon the Jewish people.  We read that “at that time your people, everyone who is found written in the book, will be rescued.”  Now, that doesn’t mean every Jewish person — it’s “everyone who is found written in the book.”  There is coming a national deliverance — “all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:26) — but those entering the kingdom must profess Jesus to be the Messiah.

Think about this book: This is a record of saved believers, those God justifies by faith.  We have already seen this in Daniel 7:10, and Moses spoke of a book God had written (Exod. 32:32–33).  The psalmist knew of the book of the living (Psa. 69:28), and Malachi spoke of a book of remembrance (Mal. 3:16).  Jesus told the seventy to “rejoice that your names are recorded in heaven” (Luke 10:20).  John sees the book of life repeatedly (Rev. 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27), and those whose names are not found there are thrown into the lake of fire.  As such, this is a record of the redeemed.

God will save his elect in this time of crisis.  One person explains it this way: Daniel’s people will be delivered by Michael’s intervention, and those who sleep will be raised.[8]  Some will be martyred, especially among the Gentiles, but also the Jews, for their profession of Messiah.  But even they will be rescued, as we see next:

Second, the Resurrections of the End Times (v. 2)
And many of those who sleep in the dust of the ground will awake, these to everlasting life, but the others to reproach and everlasting contempt.

Those whose names are written in God’s book will be rescued.  This means that survival depends on one’s covenant relationship with God, not on present circumstances and crises.  If a person dies in the Lord, he will awaken to everlasting life, while those who die in unrepentance will awake to everlasting disgrace and contempt.  This is the greatest reversal of fortunes in history, with the arrogant and powerful receiving shame while the oppressed who trusted God receive vindication.

Let’s consider this in a bit more detail.  “Sleep” is a euphemism for death, as the phrase “in the dust of the ground” makes obvious.[9]  Now, there is a theory that the soul itself sleeps in the ground because of language like this.  However, that isn’t how we should understand it.

The soul leaves the body.  For instance, the apostle Paul said to “be absent from the body” is “to be at home with the Lord” (2 Cor. 5:8), and that to depart from the flesh is to “be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).  Yet, he also used the euphemism “sleep” for death (1 Cor. 11:30; 15:6, 18, 20, 51; 1 Thess. 4:13–15; 5:10).  Scripture uses “sleep” to symbolize death of the body (not the soul), and the “awaking” then is a symbol of the body’s resurrection.  The soul does not lose consciousness.

Incidentally, we heard that same hope this morning from 2 Corinthians 5:1–12. The current tent of our dwelling is temporary, but we will have an eternal building from God.  Daniel is now showing us the day when that tent is not merely folded away, but raised in glory — or, for the unbelieving, raised to disgrace.

This was an OT expectation.  As Wiersbe notes,

When Abraham went to Mount Moriah to offer up Isaac, he believed that God could raise his son from the dead (Gen. 22; Heb. 11:19).  Job expected to see God in his resurrection body (Job 19:25–27), and this anticipation was shared by the writers of the Psalms (17:15; 49:15; 71:20).  The prophets believed in a future resurrection (Isa. 25:7; Hosea 13:14).[10]

This is what the saints of the OT looked forward to happening.

As such, this is how our Lord Jesus understood it.  In John 5:28–29 He said, “Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear His voice, and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.”  Similarly, in John 11, as He is about to raise Lazarus, Martha also states the doctrine — “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day” (John 11:24).  Jesus not only answers with affirmation, but says, “I am the resurrection and the life; he who believes in Me will live even if he dies, and everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die.  Do you believe this?” (John 11:25–26).  He then proved the claim by reviving dead Lazarus, demonstrating that He would personally be the one raising the dead righteousness to resurrected life.

Our bodies will become like that of the resurrected Christ.  This is the kind of awakening that the rest of the New Testament develops.  This is the ultimate deliverance Jesus works for His people.

Before we talk about that, though, it’s important to note that there’s more than one resurrection mentioned here.  We read that the others awake “to disgrace and everlasting contempt.”  The NASB 95 footnote on “contempt” gives the literal sense meaning of “abhorrence.”  The Hebrew word occurs only one other time in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 66:24, where the redeemed “will go forth and look on the corpses of the men who have transgressed against Me.  For their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched; and they will be an abhorrence to all mankind.”  Isaiah explains what Daniel means here.[11]

There are a few people who would really like for hell to be an annihilation of the soul.  Some Christians think annihilation is somehow kinder than eternal conscious torment, and unbelievers who refuse to turn to the Lord likewise prefer to think they will not have to face conscious consequences.  However, our Lord illustrated that, when the spirit of an unbeliever departs, it finds itself in a place of conscious torment (Luke 16:22–23).[12]  Daniel here won’t allow for another view — the contempt the wicked face is just as eternal as the life believers receive.  The same word “everlasting” stands over both destinies, meaning that, if life is unending, so is the disgrace.

Now, this text may make it seem like these two resurrections occur at the same time.  Yet, it’s not unusual for Old Testament prophecy to present events side-by-side, even if they’re separated by a considerable span of time.  We’ve already considered this in this series.  Daniel is saying that after the tribulation many — both righteous and wicked — will be raised, but he doesn’t say these events occur at the same time.[13]  As we’ll see, one comes before the kingdom, while the other happens afterward.

The main point is that death fails to have the last word.  The body that sleeps will awake from the grave.  For those who are written in the book, that awakening is to everlasting life.  That brings me to the final point:

Third, the Glory of the End Times (v. 3)
And those who have insight will shine brightly like the brightness of the expanse of heaven, and those who lead the many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever.

Here, we have the promise that the saints will be vindicated.  There are those with “insight,” terminology we’ve already encountered in Daniel (Dan 11:33, 35).  In this case, these are those who understand when the time comes (12:10).  To be clear, insight isn’t personal cleverness, but a true knowledge that arises by faith in God’s Word.[14]  It belongs to all who recognize the truth of God and act upon it.

They “shine forth” with God’s glory as a reward for their faithfulness in the time of crisis and distress.[15]  To shine in glory is a privilege of all the saved,[16] of course, since the “host of heaven” and “stars” can symbolize the people of God (Dan. 8:10).  Yet, these tribulation saints are noteworthy for their influence of others for righteousness.  Therefore, they will shine like stars in varying capacities of light.

Of course, there’s a sense in which we can all shine on earth now, like John the Baptist (John 5:35).  “A man’s wisdom now makes his face to shine (Eccles. 8:1),”[17] and “he who is wise wins souls” (Prov. 11:30).  We can display heavenly wisdom by proclaiming the truth and leading people to righteousness.

That’s what we see with the saints living through the tribulation: influencing others for the righteousness of the kingdom.  While they may face persecution and even martyrdom, they proclaim the truth of God.  The Lord remembers them.

Where is the potential reward?  The resurrection to life begins the Messianic Kingdom, a reign anticipated throughout the OT.  One author explains this way:

The Father has promised a kingdom to His Son (Ps. 2; Luke 1:30–33), and He will keep His promise.  One day Jesus will deliver that promised kingdom up to the Father (1 Cor. 15:24).  Knowing the Father’s promise, Satan tempted Jesus by offering Him all the kingdoms of the world in return for His worship (Matt. 4:8–10); and Jesus refused.  Jesus affirmed the kingdom promise to His disciples (Luke 22:29–30), and when they asked Him when it would be fulfilled (Acts 1:6–8), He only told them not to speculate about the times but to get busy doing the work He left them to do.  However, He didn’t deny the fact that one day there would be a kingdom.  Paul used the return of Christ and the establishment of the future kingdom to motivate Timothy in his ministry (2 Tim. 4:1ff), and this promise ought to be a motivating factor in our lives.”[18]

No time frame is given to this period in the OT, but in Revelation, this period is identified as being one thousand years in length six times.  There are, of course, those who take this round number to be figurative, and they go further to say that the entire description is an allegory of the present church age.  They don’t exactly deny the existence of the Messianic Kingdom, but because they deny the physical descriptions of it, they are known as amillennialists.[19]  A variation on that amillennialism is postmillennialism — the belief that we, through our efforts in this age, usher in the kingdom of peace at some point of full gospel penetration.  Both views have Christ returning again after this age is done.

By contrast, we hold a view that we believe is consistent with the plain reading of the text.  There will be a period of Great Tribulation followed by the resurrection of the saints.  After that is the millennial reign of Christ.  We also believe this matches what the Book of Revelation, where the Tribulation of the earth culminates with the coming of Christ in Revelation 19 and the judgment of the Antichrist; that is followed by Revelation 20 and the binding of Satan for 1,000 years, with the saints receiving what is specifically called “the first resurrection” (v. 5).  The unrighteous dead only receive their resurrection after the millennium (vv. 11–15).  So, there is tribulation, Christ’s return, the resurrection to life, the millennial reign, and then judgment of the dead.

There is more that happens, but those are the overlapping movements.  The resurrected saints (and those who survive the tribulation) come into the kingdom.  It is there that the rewards come: Jesus said faithfulness to Him today leads to reward and ministry in the future kingdom (Matt. 13:43; 19:27–28; 25:14–30; Luke 19:12–27), and we will share in His coming glory.[20]

So, there is a great coming hope for these end times!

Conclusion
We should not be afraid of the end times, disquieting as they may be.  Rather, we should have assurance and even anticipation!

Daniel 12:1–3 has given us three reasons.  Yes, there will be an unprecedented  crisis on earth, but Michael will stand and the people written in the book will be rescued.  While some may die, they can know that their bodies will soon awake, and the unrighteous will awake to everlasting contempt.  Moreover, those who have insight will shine as beacons forever.
So, don’t be afraid.  If you are, make certain your name is in the book.  Jesus Christ is the resurrection and the life.  The question He put to Martha is the question you should ask of yourself: “Do you believe this?”

If you are a believer, know that your work isn’t in vain.  As Paul said, “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Rom. 8:18).  Take the long view of hardship in this life as you dedicate yourself to work that will make you shine.

text:
The popular historical consensus surrounding the military operations in Georgia during the summer of 1864 presents an incomplete analysis by treating the choices available to high command as a simple binary choice between a cautious commander focused on preservation and an aggressive successor focused on frontal assaults. 

Relying on popular soldier memoirs from the ranks provides an invaluable window into tactical morale and the lived experience of the trenches, but it lacks the necessary vanguard perspective required to judge strategic and political necessity. An objective, assessment requires looking beyond to examine the structural realities that governed the western theater. By evaluating the collapse of civil military communication, the mechanical realities of modern railroad logistics, and the crushing pressure of the political calendar, the fatal flaws of a purely defensive strategy become entirely manifest, weaving these three pillars into the definitive arc of the campaign's failure.

The narrative celebrating a purely defensive approach rests on the fundamental premise that preserving the field army was the primary duty of the commander. This perspective fails to recognize that a field army in a war of national survival cannot operate as a self preserving entity detached from the state it serves. An army exists to secure territory, defend key manufacturing hubs, and protect logistical choke points. By repeatedly conducting turning movements that surrendered the industrial capacity and agricultural wealth of the region, the defensive strategy traded away vital resources. Giving up geographical space for time is only a valid strategy if that time is actively employed to build a concentrated counteroffensive or decisively sever the enemy's lines of communication. Simply ceding the strategic initiative at every step allowed the opposing army to advance unimpeded, eventually pinning the defending forces against the very urban fortifications they were supposed to protect.

The first major pillar of this failure was the total collapse of civil military communication, driven by professional reticence at the theater level. The official telegraphic logs directly contradict the myth that the executive branch removed the commander out of personal impatience or sudden anger. The removal was the culmination of weeks of evasive, non committal correspondence. When the executive explicitly requested a specific plan of operations to anticipate events, the telegraphic reply offered no concrete operational strategy, stating only that operations must depend upon those of the enemy. For an executive administration watching its premier western army retreat over 100 miles in under three months, this response was an admission of strategic passivity. A sovereign government cannot allow a theater commander to retreat across an entire state in absolute silence while a vital political and industrial hub faces siege. The executive branch understood that losing the city without a fight would guarantee the political re election of the opposing administration and destroy any remaining hope for independence.

Furthermore, the argument that the defensive strategy successfully stretched enemy logistics falls apart under close inspection of the mechanical realities of modern railroad logistics. The invading forces depended entirely on a single track railroad line running hundreds of miles back to its main base. Logistical reports from military railroad operations demonstrate that this overextended supply system was a theoretical vulnerability that the defending forces utterly failed to exploit. 

To maintain this lifeline, a highly organized logistical apparatus was utilized, including thousands of men to operate the rolling stock and specialized construction laborers who rebuilt bridges and tracks within hours of any disruption. The massive volume of supplies required a minimum of 160 train cars per day arriving at the front lines. If the entire goal of the retreat was to exploit this overextension, the execution was remarkably deficient. There was a consistent failure to coordinate concentrated cavalry operations to permanently disrupt the line. Because defending assets were kept closely tied to the infantry lines, the enemy construction corps easily repaired minor track damage, ensuring that supply lines remained secure and operational throughout the entire advance.

The most critical flaw in the defensive strategy, however, was its absolute blindness to the crushing pressure of the political calendar of the opposing government. By late August 1864, offensives across multiple theaters had ground into bloody, protracted stalemates. Public morale in the north had plummeted, and the administration was convinced that it would be defeated in the upcoming November election by a platform calling for an immediate cessation of hostilities. The depth of this political anxiety is preserved in official memoranda from the period, which stated it seemed exceedingly probable that the current administration would not be re elected, necessitating a cooperation with the president elect to save the union between the election and the inauguration. 

This primary evidence demonstrates exactly how close the defense was to achieving its political goals through a military stalemate. However, maintaining a stalemate required convincing the public that the invading armies were making no progress. A continuous, silent retreat conveyed the exact opposite impression, providing a clear visual narrative of progress. When the city finally fell in September, it completely broke the political deadlock, instantly revitalized morale, and guaranteed a landslide victory in November.

The subsequent tactical decisions made by the aggressive replacement commander were undoubtedly disastrous. Frontal assaults against fortified positions caused rapid, unsustainable attrition within the ranks, decimating the officer corps in a single afternoon during later operations. However, criticizing reckless aggression does not automatically validate strategic passivity. Both command approaches represented a dual failure of leadership in the theater. One managed a slow death by strategic strangulation, while the other simply accelerated the timeline. Framing the campaign as a simple battle between defensive intelligence and offensive incompetence misses the broader historical truth. By the time the army reached the outskirts of the key industrial city in total silence, the strategic parameters of the entire campaign had already been lost, broken by the intersection of fractured communication, industrial logistics, and an unyielding political clock.

text:
BEAUTY IN THE GROTESQUE

On the 1819 Illinois frontier, a family’s deepest shame becomes a public commodity.

Hidden away in a rotting loft by parents who only ever called him It, twenty-one-year-old Gideon has known nothing of the world outside a narrow box and the sound of floorboards overhead. He has never been touched with kindness, never walked the open grass, and never heard his own true name spoken without a sneer.

Until the day his parents offer him the one thing he thought was impossible: hope. They tell him they are taking him to a doctor.

Instead, the frontier doesn't want to heal Gideon—they want to stare. And when showman P.T. Barnum enters the fold, a cruel local secret is transformed into a national spectacle. 

Beauty in the Grotesque is a visceral historical horror about innocence betrayed, entertainment fueled by human exploitation, and a world that chose to look at a human being and see only a ticket stub.
